Trouble deciding which backpacking tent would be right for you? Here's my two cents.
Most hikers today agree a 2 person tent is worth the small weight penalty The extra space and comfort are worth it so all the tents here are 2p. If ultralight is your goal there are some fine 1 person tents that will do the job.

These are all 3 season tents. If you have need for a 4 season winter tent...What the fuck is wrong with you?

Types of tents

  • Freestanding: These tents have what is equivalent to a skeleton (aluminum poles) that will hold the tent up. Still requires stakes tho.
  • Non-Freestanding: Many hikers today carry trekking poles. Theres a good variety of tents available that can use trekking poles to substiture for tent poles giving you a nice weight savings.
  • Single Wall: Tent made from one piece of fabric. Subject to condesation problems but very light weight. Good for dry trails in the desert etc.
  • Double Wall: Tent with an inner wall that usually contianing some mesh and an outer waterproof fly. No condensation problems but a bit heavier.
  • Nylon: Cheap, strong but heavier fabric.
  • Dyneema: Very expensive. Not as durable as nylon but very lightweight.

My favorite tents:

  • Nemo Hornet. Nylon, freestanding, double wall tent. 1 pound 14.3 oz $369.95 on REI. Side entry, making access much easier. Had a friend carry one the length of the PCT with no problems. Green color makes it a great tent for stealth camping. Dam good tent.
  • Big Agnes HV UL2. Probably the most popular tent on long trails today. Freestanding, nylon, double wall. 1 pound 15 oz. $349.95 on REI. Front entry which is a pain in the ass.
  • MSR Hubba Bubba. Nylon, freestanding, double wall. 3 pound 8 oz. 449.95 on REI. Side entry, heavy duty tent. Great tent for bike or canoe touring where a little extra weight is not a problem. Good tent.
  • ZPacks Duplex. Dyneema, non-freestanding, single wall tent. 20 oz. Side entry but expensive. $600 on ZPacks. Probably the second most popular tent on long trails.

This is hardly a comprehensive list. The possibilities are almost endless. In the east you can use a hammock. Some ultralighters use only a tarp. One famous hiker had a tarp/poncho combination eliminating the need to carry rain gear. In the end the choices seem to be somewhat personal and shopping and researching gear is part of the fun.
